questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two gastric orifices in terms of sphincters?
options: Both have anatomical and physiological sphincters
The cardiac orifice has no anatomical sphincter but has a physiological one; the pyloric orifice has both
The cardiac orifice has an anatomical sphincter only; the pyloric has a physiological sphincter only
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a physiological sphincter at the cardiac orifice, while the pyloric orifice has anatomical and physiological sphincters.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page states that the cardiac orifice lacks an anatomical sphincter but has a physiological one, whereas the pyloric orifice has both.

questions.stem: Where does the stomach have its described bare area?
options: On the anterior surface near the pylorus
On the posterior surface close to the cardiac orifice
On the inferior surface near the angular notch
questions.explanation: The stomach is generally covered by peritoneum except for a bare area on its posterior surface near the cardiac orifice.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page specifies the bare area on the posterior surface close to the cardiac orifice.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, which vagal nerves provide parasympathetic supply to the stomach?
options: Anterior and posterior gastric nerves, from the left and right vagus respectively
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior gastric nerves are identified as vagal branches from the left and right vagus, respectively.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page assigns parasympathetic supply to anterior and posterior gastric nerves from left and right vagus, respectively.

questions.stem: How does the duodenal mucosa differ between its first part and the remainder, as described in the lecture?
options: It is folded in the first part and smooth throughout the rest
It is smooth in the first part; the remainder forms plicae circulares
It has villi only in the first part
It is smooth throughout all four parts
questions.explanation: The first part is described as smooth, while the rest of the duodenum has folds called plicae circulares.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page explicitly contrasts smooth mucosa in the first part with plicae circulares in the rest.

questions.stem: Which pair of arterial sources supplies the duodenum across its foregut–midgut transition?
options: Coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery
Inferior mesenteric artery and coeliac trunk
Renal arteries and superior mesenteric artery
Hepatic artery and inferior mesenteric artery
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies coeliac supply from the foregut and superior mesenteric supply from the midgut.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page states that duodenal supply comes from the coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery, reflecting its embryological divisions.

questions.stem: Which mesenteric arterial-arcade pattern is characteristic of the ileum in the lecture's comparison?
options: Simple arcades, usually one or two
A single direct artery without arcades
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts the jejunum's simple arcades with complicated arterial arcades in the ileum.
questions.sourceEvidence: The comparison table describes ileal arcades as complicated and jejunal arcades as simple (one or two).

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the hindgut territory defined in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut, extending in the lecture's definition from the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon to the upper half of the anal canal.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page assigns the hindgut territory to the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Which description correctly identifies the two surfaces of the spleen?
options: Medial diaphragmatic surface and lateral visceral surface
Medial visceral surface containing the hilum and lateral diaphragmatic surface
Anterior renal surface and posterior gastric surface
Superior visceral surface and inferior diaphragmatic surface
questions.explanation: The medial surface is visceral and contains the hilum; the lateral surface is related to the diaphragm.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page labels the medial surface as visceral with the hilum and the lateral surface as diaphragmatic.

questions.stem: Which structures are contained in the lienorenal ligament according to the lecture?
options: Splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas
Common bile duct and portal vein
Left gastric vessels and the stomach fundus
questions.explanation: The lienorenal ligament connects the spleen with the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page states the lienorenal ligament contains the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail.

questions.stem: Which structure separates the right and left anatomical lobes of the liver posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The lecture assigns the ligamentum venosum to the posterior separation of the right and left lobes.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page lists ligamentum venosum posteriorly, ligamentum teres inferiorly, and falciform ligament superiorly and anteriorly.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the base of the triangular bare area of the liver?
options: Groove for the inferior vena cava
questions.explanation: The base of the triangular bare area is formed by the groove for the inferior vena cava.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page defines the bare area's base as the IVC groove, its apex as the right triangular ligament, and its boundaries as the coronary ligaments.

questions.stem: At the porta hepatis, which structure is positioned posteriorly in the lecture's arrangement?
options: Right and left hepatic artery branches
Right and left portal vein branches
questions.explanation: The portal vein branches are posterior; the hepatic ducts are anterior and hepatic artery branches are in the middle.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page gives the porta hepatis arrangement as ducts anterior, artery middle, and portal vein posterior, alongside nerves and lymphatics.

questions.stem: The ligamentum venosum is the obliterated remnant of which fetal vessel?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum venosum is the obliterated ductus venosus; the ligamentum teres is the remnant of the left umbilical vein.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page directly identifies ligamentum venosum as obliterated ductus venosus and contrasts it with ligamentum teres.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly names the three parts of the common bile duct described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The common bile duct is divided into supraduodenal, retroduodenal and infraduodenal parts.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page identifies the CBD's three parts using these names after describing its course.

questions.stem: Which statement about the gall bladder's peritoneal covering is correct according to the lecture?
options: It is covered on its under surface only, while the fundus is completely covered
It is covered only on its superior surface, including the fundus
It is completely covered except at the neck
questions.explanation: The lecture states that the gall bladder is covered by peritoneum on its under surface, with the fundus completely covered.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page describes the gall bladder's peritoneum as covering the under surface only, except that the fundus is completely covered.

questions.stem: Which pancreatic part is embedded in the splenic hilum and passes within the lienorenal ligament?
questions.explanation: The pancreatic tail extends to the splenic hilum and lies within the lienorenal ligament.
questions.sourceEvidence: The page states that the tail is embedded in the splenic hilum and passes inside the lienorenal ligament.
